# Instructions

This week you learned about tidying and joining data sets with the tidyr (pronounced tidy-R) and dplyr packages.

Joining data sets can be deceptively tricky. It is important to keep in mind that prepping and inspecting the tables you're working with *before* you do a join is often more important (and takes more time) than doing the join itself.

You'll use some of these skills in the milestone to the right.

To learn more about the variables contained in the data sets, refer to the data dictionaries for `sp500` (https://rstudio.github.io/academy-tidyverse-stock-portfolios/assets/sp500_dictionary.html) and `sectors` (https://rstudio.github.io/academy-tidyverse-stock-portfolios/assets/sectors_dictionary.html).

Remember that all tidyverse packages have already been installed for you but you will need to *load* the ones you want to use.

## Tidy and join

In this milestone, you'll first tidy a data set that covers the individual stocks in the S&P 500. Then, you'll join it with sector information and compute the total daily price for each sector. To do this, you'll need to use the data in `sp500.csv` alongside `sectors.csv`. Both data sets are stored in your `data/` directory.

### Part 2 - Tidy the table

Take a look at the `sp500` data set. Notice that the `event` column contains the _names_ of variables (`open`, `high`, `low`, `close`, `adjusted`), and the `price` column contains their values. To make this data tidy, each of those events should be its own column.

Use a tidyr function in the code chunk below to pivot `sp500` so that each event becomes its own column. Save the result as `sp500_tidy`; we will use it in Part 3.

### Part 3 - Join tables and summarize

Run the code below to see a table.

```{r}
#| label: recreate-this
#| message: false
solution <- readr::read_csv("data/milestone04.csv")
solution
```

Your task is to use what you've learned about the dplyr package to transform `sp500_tidy` and `sectors` into this table. You will need to:

1. Join the two data sets. (Hint: which variable can you join on? You may want to use `anti_join()` to check for any mismatched observations before joining.)
2. Group by `sector` and `date`
3. Compute a `daily_total` summary, the sum of `adjusted` for each group (Hint: remove `NA`s from `adjusted` before adding them up)

Work in the code chunk below. Save the result as `sector_prices`.

```{r}

```

Run the following code chunk to test whether you have the same answer as the solution:

```{r}
#| label: compare
#| eval: false
waldo::compare(sector_prices, solution, tolerance = 1e-4)
```

### Part 4 - Visualize

Now that you have computed the total daily price for each sector, you can compare the sectors over time. Run the chunk below to visualize `sector_prices`.

```{r}
#| label: visualize-sectors
#| eval: false
sector_prices |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = date, y = daily_total, color = sector)) +
    geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Total daily price by sector")
```

## Extension

Using the code chunk below, investigate a single research question about this data, using the skills you have learned this week and in previous weeks of Academy. Some ideas:

1. Create a visualization using the joined data from the milestone recreation; refine the visualization (subset data, adjust graph, etc.) at least once as you begin a further investigation of the data. In your work, use at least one data transformation step and one graph to start addressing your questions.
2. Using `sector_prices`, compute the Cumulative Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) for each sector, using `((last(daily_total) / first(daily_total)) - 1) * 100`. Which sector outperformed the rest?
3. Choose 2-3 companies _from the same sector_ in the joined data and compare their performance across a time window of interest. (This could be open / high / low / close price data, shares held, or multiple variables.)
4. Use `tidyquant::tq_performance()` to find some performance statistics for the stocks in the `sp500_tidy` data set. Along with another metric of interest, consider calculating the Sharpe ratio, one of the most widely used methods for measuring risk-adjusted relative returns, for each symbol. You can learn more about the Sharpe ratio here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharpe_ratio
